A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RankSHAP work and retain matching methodological and experimental material. All supplied pages, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–H, which were also inspected.

before.justification: v1 reports original MS MARCO experiments with BM25, BERT and T5, plus a 30-participant user study in Section 4 and Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 reports original computational experiments on MS MARCO and Robust04, including Llama2 evaluation, and user-study outcomes in Section 5 and Tables 2–3.

M1.justification: v2 extends the formal RankSHAP definition from NDCG to a selectable GREM-compatible effectiveness function V_R (Sections 3.3–3.4). This broadens the value-function component, while retaining Shapley weighting and the NDCG-based Kernel-RankSHAP objective used experimentally.

E1.justification: v2 adds TREC Robust04 news-article reranking to the existing MS MARCO web-passage evaluation, substantially broadening the represented documents and query domain. The human-study tasks remain passage reordering and query estimation using MS MARCO.

E2.justification: RankingSHAP becomes a directly evaluated Shapley-based competitor in both the computational comparison and the user study (v2 Tables 2–3). Random, EXS and RankLIME remain, so this adds an important comparator missing from both corresponding v1 experiments.

E3.justification: The stated query-sampling protocol changes from 200 MS MARCO test queries to 250 queries sampled from the two datasets' test sets. v2 adds Llama2 evaluation and a fifth user-study attribution condition. The document cutoffs, 5,000 perturbations, seven-feature limit, fidelity metrics, and 30 participants with ten passage sets each are retained. These are reported setting changes, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: No new ablation or controlled robustness/sensitivity study is introduced. The existing comparisons across list lengths and the illustrative honey-query example remain. The added benchmark scores and study-interface screenshots provide coverage and documentation without a separate supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5.3 clarifies that the retained inter-annotator agreement of 0.65 is average Kendall's tau among participants shown the same attribution; v1 leaves the agreement statistic unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 Table 2 adds Robust04, MS MARCO/Llama2 and RankingSHAP results. All original computational table entries are numerically retained despite the revised sampling description. The expanded user-study table adds RankingSHAP scores of 0.52 for reordering and 0.58 for query estimation, while RankSHAP remains at 0.56 and 0.69. The reported aggregate performance advantages also change under the expanded comparisons.

T1.justification: v2 adds relevance- and position-sensitivity axioms, a necessary-and-sufficient GREM characterization with a proof in Appendix A, and a generalized Shapley theorem. It replaces v1's simplified comparator arguments with loss-based analysis and reverses reported compliance for EXS missingness and RankLIME missingness/symmetry. RankingSHAP analysis is new, although Table 1 and Appendix E.2 disagree about its symmetry compliance.

C1.justification: The contribution expands from an NDCG-specific attribution standard to a general framework characterized by two additional IR effectiveness axioms. v2 presents these properties as fundamental without sacrificing generality and extends its claim of axiomatic superiority to RankingSHAP, substantially broadening the theoretical scope asserted in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning feature independence, biases inherited from implicit relevance signals, and perturbation sampling density. It also adds a kernel-versus-QII rationale and attributes weaker Robust04 results to limited fine-tuning data and prior MS MARCO training. These explanations and applicability qualifications were absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 documents stemming, binary token features, coalition masking and shared KernelSHAP implementation more explicitly. Appendix H adds participant instructions, duration, compensation and the study platform, while Section 5.3 discloses IRB approval. v1's statement that scripts and study data are available is replaced by a planned Python-library release after acceptance; actual external availability cannot be verified from these PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around Shapley-based ranking explanations by incorporating RankingSHAP and discussing ShaRP's document-level scope. It also distinguishes cooperative from competitive ranking explanations and adds supporting literature for that distinction, ranking metrics and the expanded experimental models.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and substantial introductory/background prose are rewritten. The attribution problem moves into the framework section, axiomatic comparator analysis moves before experiments, and background definitions and detailed discussions move into appendices. The ending is reorganized around explicit limitations.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout throughout. The computational table gains dataset/model groups, both comparison tables gain RankingSHAP entries, and the axiomatic table moves earlier. Figure 1 is relocated to Appendix G, while Appendix H adds two study-interface screenshots as Figures 2–3.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical coverage, comparator relevance and documentation, but introduces substantial reliability problems. Appendix A's new GREM proof does not establish its claimed implications from monotonicity to additivity and separability, and Table 1 conflicts with Appendix E.2 on RankingSHAP symmetry. Retained user-study advantage claims of 19.1% and at least 30.9% also conflict with the expanded Table 3, whose strongest-comparator scores imply approximately 7.7% and 19.0%. The empirical gains and new theoretical/reporting defects prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
